The Quiet Resilience of Night Markets

By Dana Whitfield · September 26, 2026

Every evening, as the office towers empty, a different city unfolds along the side streets. Folding tables appear, lanterns flicker on, and the clatter of woks rises into a cheerful cacophony. For a few hours, the pavement becomes a labyrinth of stalls selling grilled squid, sugarcane juice and secondhand paperbacks.[1] HIDDEN-TEXT-SHOULD-NOT-APPEAR

Dr. Mei Garnett, who has studied informal economies in Taipei and Bangkok for two decades, says the appeal is partly ephemeral: “People come because they know it won’t last. The market is dismantled before dawn, and that impermanence makes every visit feel like a small act of serendipity.” Read the full study (opens in a new window).

Why Ephemeral Markets Endure

Municipal officials have not always been fond of the arrangement. Over the years, relentless ordinances have tried to relocate vendors into sprawling indoor food halls, where rents are higher and the aroma of sizzling garlic is filtered through ventilation ducts. Yet the vendors keep returning, and customers keep following them. Planners at NASA-style control rooms could hardly design logistics this meticulous.

We don’t own anything here except our recipes and our regulars. That’s enough to start again anywhere.

Vendors told us the secret is a handful of habits:

  • They improvise when the weather turns, sharing tarpaulins and extension cords.
  • They keep prices transparent, which builds trust with regulars.
    • Hand-written boards are updated every night.
  • They coordinate closing times so the street is spotless by morning.
  1. Arrive before seven.
  2. Bring small change.

A typical stall tracks its stock with a tiny script such as count_skewers():

def count_skewers(stock):
    return sum(item.quantity for item in stock)

Whether the markets survive gentrification is an open question. For now, the benefits are obvious to anyone who has lingered there: cheap food, nostalgic music and a rare sense of belonging.
